newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - July 21.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - July 21.

text.p: The following stories were reported in Monday's electronic version of The Wall Street Journal:
* FCC rules on how local phone companies must open their networks to rivals were thrown out by a federal appeals court.
* Bell Atlantic and NYNEX agreed to a number of provisions aimed at fostering competition in their northeast phone markets.
* The U.S. trade gap grew in May to $10.23 billion.
* At least four Columbia/HCA employees have been subpoenaed by a grand jury.
* Stocks fell Friday in heavy trading.
* Securities regulators are moving toward ending the practice of forcing all Wall Street employment disputes into industry-sponsored arbitration.
* Oppenheimer is close to reaching an agreement to be acquired by Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce in a deal valued at $525 million
* Rite Aid has agreed to acquire two closely held drugstore chains in Alabama and Louisianna.
* Sprint plans to acquire Paranet for $425 million.
* Walt Disney is near a pact to buy the independent record label Mammoth Records.
* IBP posted a 61 percent drop in second quarter earnings.
* Montgomery Ward rejected a revised offer for its Signature Group direct marketing subsidiary from HFS.
* AMR 's American Airlines and British Airways said they aim to forge closer ties with Spain's state-owned Iberia Airlines.
* Possible "pay-to-play" abuses in the public retirement fund business will be investigated by a California Senate committee.
* Urohealth Systems said it has revised the terms of its agreement to acquire Imagyn Medical for stock.
* Pherin Pharmaceuticals agreed with a unit of Dutch chemical company Akzo to develop medicines that would convert a new found apparent sixth sense into a pathway to treat a variety of maladies.
* A stake in Grundig of 43 percent was acquired by a European-investor group.
* Wall Street financial firms, looking for a piece of the burgeoning junk-bond market, are offering guarantees that could come back to bite them.
* One camp on Wall Street is convinced that Apple Computer is going to disappear, while another camp envisions a takeover at $20-plus a share.
((-- New York Newsdesk 212-859-1610))
